tagline: A winged snail with a ruthless appetite
summary: The sea angel is a shell-less snail that 'flies' through cold Arctic and North Atlantic waters by flapping two wing-like lobes of its foot. Its see-through body glows with orange-red organs. Gentle as it looks, it is a specialist hunter that pulls sea butterflies out of their shells.

stats.size: Up to about 7–8.5 cm in the north; much smaller further south
stats.range: Arctic Ocean and cold North Atlantic, south at least to the Sargasso Sea
stats.diet: Almost exclusively sea butterflies (Limacina helicina and L. retroversa)

facts.title: Snail with wings
facts.text: Sea angels are snails without shells. They swim by beating two wing-like flaps of the foot, and use gravity-sensing organs to keep upright in the water.

facts.title: A one-dish diet
facts.text: Adults eat almost nothing but sea butterflies, their shelled pteropod cousins. In Svalbard, researchers describe the sea butterfly Limacina helicina as its only prey.

facts.title: Grab, hook, extract
facts.text: Three pairs of finger-like 'buccal cones' shoot out of its mouth to grip a sea butterfly's shell. Chitin hooks then pull the soft body out, and the sea angel swallows it whole.

facts.title: A year without food
facts.text: In a lab experiment, sea angels from Svalbard survived 356 days with no food at all, shrinking from about 22 to 12 mm while living off stored fats.

facts.title: Whale food
facts.text: Baleen whales and fishes eat sea angels, and sailors historically nicknamed them 'whale-food'.

notes: Both photos are of live/fresh animals photographed in containers (black background), not in situ — labelled 'specimen'. The NOAA photo is from Alaska (AFSC); Wikipedia notes North Pacific Clione are now often treated as C. elegantissima, so that ID follows the photographer's label. WoRMS order for Clionidae returned as Pteropoda. The Walla Walla Salish Sea page (also describing buccal cones) was not cited because it treats NE Pacific animals as C. limacina. Size, depth, range, buccal-cone and 'whale-food' facts via Wikipedia (citing WoRMS, Lalli & Gilmer 1989, Böer et al.).
